title: Januarius (19 September)
hookLine: a bishop-martyr of Naples whose relic of blood is said to liquefy; the Church hasn't ruled on it
tomorrow: Andrew Kim Taegon and companions (20 September)

cards: The cathedral in Naples is packed, and everyone is waiting. Up front, a priest holds a small glass reliquary. Inside is something dark and solid, which the people of Naples say is the dried blood of their patron saint.
The priest turns it slowly, again and again, so the crowd can see. People pray, some of them out loud, and watch to see whether, today, it will turn to liquid. When it does, a cry goes up.
When it doesn't, the city worries. Today, the bishop at the center of all that waiting. Januarius.

teach.b: First, the man. Tradition says Januarius was a bishop of Benevento, in southern Italy, killed for his faith in a Roman persecution, near Naples. Beyond that, little can be confirmed.
His relics came to Naples, and Naples took him as its own: he is the city's patron.

Second, the blood. Tradition says it was gathered after his death and kept. The vessels are kept in the cathedral, and on his feast and some other days in the year the reliquary is brought out, and the people wait.
Often, witnesses say, the dark mass turns liquid. Sometimes it doesn't. Third, what the Church says, and this matters.
The Church hasn't ruled on it. It allows the devotion, and it doesn't require anyone to believe that the change is a miracle. People have offered natural explanations, and the question stays open.
Catholics are free to hold it either way. So the center of this day isn't a verdict.
It's a city standing together, hoping.

teach.h: PRECIOUS IN THE SIGHT OF THE LORD.
teach.b: A line from the Psalms, in the Douay-Rheims, is close to the heart of it: "Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints."
Whatever happens inside that glass, Naples has kept a martyr's death close, and treated it as precious. And there's the waiting itself: a crowd with nothing to do but pray and watch together.
Some days the answer comes quickly. Some days it's slow. Some days it doesn't come at all, and they come back anyway.

how: On 19 September, and on some other days in the year, the reliquary of Saint Januarius is shown in the cathedral of Naples while the faithful pray and wait to see whether the blood liquefies; elsewhere Catholics may keep his optional memorial.

o: a pope who began the Church's new year in January
the Roman god of doors, who gave January its name
a bishop and martyr, the patron saint of Naples

p: the city that keeps his relic
dried blood said to turn liquid

s: Catholics are required to believe the blood liquefies
the Church hasn't ruled on it. it allows the devotion, and Catholics are free to hold it either way.
much of Januarius's life can't be confirmed
tradition calls him a bishop and martyr; beyond that, little is certain.
when the blood stays solid, the city worries
the people wait, and when it doesn't happen, they worry and come back anyway.

games.q: you're a Church official. people want the liquefaction declared a miracle, once and for all. what do you do?
o: let the people keep praying, and leave the question open.
games.why: the Church has left it open. the devotion goes on, and no one is required to believe it.

practice: Let the sit be a stretch of waiting, the way the crowd waits before the glass, and notice what you're waiting on in your own life, news, a change, an answer that hasn't come, holding it loosely.

Then widen the circle to anyone waiting today, by a hospital bed, by a phone, at a door. If you pray, pray for Naples and ask Saint Januarius to pray for it; if you don't, simply wait alongside them, without needing an answer.

wordCard.voice: Januarius. The bishop and martyr, patron of Naples, whose blood in a glass vessel is said to turn liquid. The Church hasn't ruled on it.

carryVoice: Your line: the people wait. A whole city, waiting together, and still hoping. Until tomorrow.

sources.q: Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints.
